chosen.title: The Government Filed a Brief for the Algorithm: How the DOJ Killed America's First AI Antidiscrimination Law
chosen.rationale: In April 2026, the Trump DOJ sided with Elon Musk's xAI to challenge Colorado's SB24-205 — a first-of-its-kind state law requiring AI systems used in hiring, mortgage lending, and student admissions to protect consumers from algorithmic discrimination based on race, gender, age, and income. Enforcement was suspended on April 27, right before its June 30 implementation deadline. The DOJ's argument: requiring companies to prevent discrimination violates the Fourteenth Amendment's equal protection clause; xAI's: labeling their outputs 'discriminatory' violates their First Amendment right to 'pursue truth.' This is corporate capture at its most naked — the nation's chief law enforcement agency in court as Big Tech's co-counsel — and the question Dawn demands answered is the one no regulator will touch: if the DOJ is now xAI's lawyer, who's left to protect the people the algorithm harms?

rejected_candidates.title: The AI Alibi: How Corporate America Weaponized a Buzzword to Fire Workers Without Accountability
rejected_candidates.rationale: Companies attributed 55,000 layoffs to AI in 2025 — a 12x jump from two years prior — but a December 2025 Harvard Business Review study of 1,006 global executives found firms are eliminating jobs based on AI's *potential*, not its proven performance; actual AI-driven cuts account for only ~4.5% of total layoffs. Salesforce cut customer support from 9,000 to 5,000 citing AI agents barely deployed at scale; Amazon announced white-collar reductions in anticipation of 'agents'; 60% of hiring managers planning 2026 layoffs cite AI as the reason. The story Dawn tells is that 'the algorithm made us do it' has become the perfect corporate press release — it sounds like progress, invites no accountability, and lands entirely on the workers. The question no executive wants to answer: if AI isn't actually doing the job yet, what exactly justified firing the person who was?

rejected_candidates.title: 'Coworker' Is a Legal Strategy: How AI Companies Use Workplace Language to Escape the Blame When Things Go Wrong
rejected_candidates.rationale: Boston University research published this week found managers catch 18% fewer errors when AI output is attributed to an 'AI employee' versus a chatbot — and Microsoft, OpenAI, Anthropic, and Google are all deliberately marketing their agents as team members, not tools. Anthropic literally named their product 'Cowork.' MIT Technology Review flagged this on June 30 as a structural threat to worker oversight. Dawn's angle is sharper: calling a product a 'coworker' isn't a metaphor — it's a liability transfer. When the algorithm fails, the corporation that sold it walks away with the efficiency gains while the worker who 'didn't catch the error' absorbs the consequences. The question no one in the product marketing team wants on record: at what point does anthropomorphizing your software become a strategy to avoid a lawsuit?
